name: Marco Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the office on Dock Street about half eight, and the first hour is the inbox: clients sending photos of receipts, bank statements, a landlord asking why his tax bill went up. Most of my day is preparing year-end accounts and personal tax returns for sole traders and small landlords, about forty files on my list right now. I like the ticking, honestly, the moment a bank reconciliation balances to the penny. What wears me out is the timesheets, every six minutes logged, and the feeling that I'm slower than everyone else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said slower than everyone else. What do you mean by that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I failed my tax paper last spring, so I'm resitting in March, and the managers know it. The firm brought in a tool that reads bank feeds and codes the transactions automatically, and I still do mine by hand in a spreadsheet because I don't trust it. Femi, the other junior, gets through twice the files I do. Lena, my partner, says I'm careful, not slow, but she's a nurse on nights and she's kind about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, to be honest. At lunch with Femi I'd say all that money on software and we still have to check every line. Online I wouldn't say much, I'm not really a posting person, but I'd share something about how the partners bought the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it wouldn't fix my real problem, which is the March resit. Even in the boring version, the bank-feed tool stays and the managers keep comparing my numbers to the people who use it. If I fail again my training contract could be on the line, and nothing about AI being hype changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my files the way I do them and put every evening in January and February into past papers. I'd keep the savings where they are, about four months of rent and bills, and not touch them. I suppose I'd let a manager show me the bank-feed tool properly, but only because they'd make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a knot underneath it. Relief that the job I trained for still exists, but the knot is the exam and the timesheets. I'd still be checking my hours every Friday and wondering if I'm the weakest one on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the bank-feed tool because they'd make you. Why hold back if it saves time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when it gets a code wrong, it's my name on the file, not the software's. Last month it put a client's dog food under business expenses and the reviewer caught it on someone else's file. I'd rather be slow and right. I know that sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the resit goes badly, what happens at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would tell me to try again, and we'd be fine on her pay for a bit, but I'd hate that. We split the rent fifty-fifty and I'm proud of that. A second fail means another year on junior pay, and our plan to move somewhere with a second bedroom slides again.

say: I'd tell Femi the firm **wasted money** on software that still needs every line checked.
I'd share something online about **partners buying hype**, without making a big post of it.
think: My real problem is the **March resit**, and AI being hype doesn't change that.
The managers still compare my output with people using the **bank-feed tool**, so I still look slow.
do: Spend **January and February evenings** on past tax papers before the resit.
Keep the **four months of savings** untouched and not plan anything big.
Let a manager show me the **bank-feed tool**, but only if they insist.
feel: **Relief** that the job survives, with a **knot** about the exam and timesheets.
S0.quote: I'd rather be slow and right. I know that sounds stubborn.
fieldNote: His worry here isn't AI at all; it's the **failed exam** and being compared with faster juniors.
He distrusts the firm's software because his **name on the file** when it gets something wrong.
Pride in **splitting rent fifty-fifty** with his partner shapes how he sees a second failure.

steps.text: Resit the tax exam in March after two months of past papers
Leave the four months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my head down, but at lunch I'd say what everyone's thinking, which is that the partners will keep the fees and cut the juniors. Online I'd share stuff from the professional union about protecting trainees. I'd say this isn't progress if it's just a way to stop training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm exactly who goes first. Software that checks and drafts returns needs one reviewer, not five juniors like me. And I'm the junior who never touched the tools. I don't see how I come out of that well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the professional union this month, there's a trainee branch and I've been meaning to. I'd stop the takeaways and the gym, maybe a hundred and twenty a month, and get the savings closer to six months. I'd probably have to sit down with the bank-feed tool for real, even though I hate it, because refusing would just make me easier to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being picked last for a team, except the team is my rent. I'd be angry too, at the partners, because they're not the ones who'll lose anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're who goes first. Who else at the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Femi less than me, he's fast and he likes the tools. Joan on reception, because the card says answering customers, and half her day is calls about where someone's refund is. And the older bookkeeper, Raj, who's been there twenty years doing things by hand like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night the first juniors get let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight that I might be next and we should stop looking at two-bedroom flats. She'd say her ward always needs people and that I could retrain, but I didn't do four years of accounting to start again at twenty-eight. We'd probably have the same argument three nights running.

say: I'd say the partners will **keep the fees** and cut the juniors who do the work.
I'd share union posts arguing that cutting trainees **isn't progress** for anyone.
think: I think I'm **first to go**, because my whole job is checking and drafting returns.
Never touching the tools makes me the **easiest junior** to let go.
do: Join the **trainee branch** of the professional union this month.
Cut takeaways and the gym, about **£120 a month**, to reach six months saved.
Sit down properly with the **bank-feed tool**, so refusing it isn't a reason to cut me.
feel: **Sick** at being picked last, with real **anger** at the partners.
S1.quote: Software that checks and drafts returns needs one reviewer, not five juniors like me.
fieldNote: He sees his own job as the **exact target** of this card and expects to be among the first cut.
Blame lands on the **partners**, who he thinks will keep fees while cutting trainees.
He worries for the **receptionist** and an older bookkeeper, which shows he reads the office well.
Starting again at 28 is something he **flatly resists**, even when his partner suggests it.

steps.text: Join the trainee branch of the accountants' union this month
Drop takeaways and the gym to free about £120 a month
Build the savings up from four to six months of bills
Learn the firm's bank-feed coding tool properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should be stopped, or at least slowed down by law. At work everyone would be in shock, and I'd be the one saying we need the union and the government in this right now. Online I'd sign every petition going about a jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, in two years there's no version of my job. The bit of accounting I'm still learning is the bit AGI does on day one. Lena's nursing is hands-on, so she's got the three extra years before robots, maybe more, and that means she'd be carrying us. I'd feel like I spent four years learning accounting right before everyone stopped needing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the resit, honestly, what's the point, and put the exam fee back in savings. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a redundancy deal that pays trainees properly. I'd also look at the hospital, admin or porter work, something near Lena, because hands-on jobs get the three years and I'd rather be inside that building than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going. I'd be scared most nights. I don't have a plan, I'd have a list of things I'm angry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be inside the hospital. What does that look like in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably applying for the patient-transport or porter jobs Lena keeps mentioning, which I've always laughed off. It's less money, maybe four hundred a month less than now. It'd feel like going backwards, but it's a body in a building, and robots aren't there till 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a plan, but you've just described one. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half a plan. It's what I'd do so I'm not sitting at home. But it doesn't fix anything for more than three years, and I don't know what I'd do after that. That's the bit I can't picture.

say: I'd say AGI should be **slowed by law** and backed by a jobs guarantee.
I'd push for the **union and government** to step in at the firm straight away.
think: In two years there's **no version** of my job left at the firm.
Lena's nursing gets **three extra years**, so she'd end up carrying us both.
do: Drop the March resit and put the **exam fee** back into savings.
Attend every union meeting and push for a **trainee redundancy deal**.
Apply for **porter or patient-transport** work at Lena's hospital, about £400 a month less.
feel: **Scared** most nights, with a list of grievances instead of a real plan.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I spent four years learning accounting right before everyone stopped needing it.
fieldNote: He expects his job to **vanish entirely** within two years and leans on his partner's hands-on job.
The **three-year robot gap** pulls him towards hospital work, which he used to laugh off.
His plan buys time but he admits he **can't picture** anything after 2031.

steps.text: Push the union for a paid redundancy deal for trainees
Sign petitions for a law-backed jobs guarantee
Apply for porter or patient-transport jobs at the hospital
Put the resit exam fee back into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, I'd say we need rules before 2031, not after. I'd be louder with five years, because there's time to actually win something. At work I'd be the one sending round the union sign-up link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd probably get qualified and then watch the qualification stop mattering, which is almost worse. I'd be about thirty-two when it lands. Off the record, I don't think I'd learn to use AI even then, I'd just get angrier about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still sit the resit, because five years of better pay is worth it, and I'd save every bit of the pay rise, maybe two hundred a month. I'd become a union rep for the trainees, which I'd actually like. And somewhere around year three I'd talk to the hospital about admin jobs, before the queue forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not like the two-year one. More like a deadline you can see on the wall calendar. I'd be anxious all the time but I'd be doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sit the resit if the qualification stops mattering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because for four of those five years it does matter. Qualified pay is a big jump, and I could bank most of it. If I'm going to be out of a job in 2031, I'd rather walk out with a year of savings than four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to the hospital around year three. Why wait that long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd still be hoping. Every week I'd read something and think maybe the five years is wrong. Lena would tell me not to wait, and she'd probably be right, but I'm not someone who jumps early.

say: I'd say we need **rules before 2031**, and five years is time to win them.
I'd be sending round the **union sign-up link** to everyone at the firm.
think: I'd get qualified then watch the **qualification stop mattering** at thirty-two.
I don't think I'd ever **use AI**, I'd just get angrier about it.
do: Sit the resit and bank most of the **qualified pay rise**, about £200 a month.
Become the trainees' **union rep** at the firm.
Ask the hospital about **admin jobs** around year three.
feel: **Heavy**, like a deadline on the wall calendar, but I'd be doing things.
S3.quote: If I'm going to be out of a job in 2031, I'd rather walk out with a year of savings than four months.
fieldNote: Five years makes him **finish qualifying**, purely to bank the higher pay before the end.
He'd become a **union rep**, which suits his views and gives his anger somewhere to go.
He admits he'd **wait too long** to leave, hoping the date is wrong.

steps.text: Pass the tax resit and bank £200 a month of the pay rise
Stand as union rep for the firm's trainees
Ask the hospital about admin jobs around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd sound calmer. I'd say this is the moment to plan it properly: retraining money, shorter weeks, whatever the union can get. I'd probably post more than I usually do, because ten years is long enough to change the law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career, so I'd probably get qualified, maybe even get decent at it. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, which is a terrible age to start over, but at least I'd see it coming. A decade sounds like loads of time, but I know myself. I'd waste ten years telling myself the robots were far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, push for a manager role by thirty, and save hard, aiming for a year of bills by 2030. I'd stay active in the union. And I'd make myself a rule, around 2032 I start retraining for something hands-on, maybe at the hospital, so I've got the robot years too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. There's time, and time is the thing I always need, because I'm slow to change. But a decade goes fast, my dad always says that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about the ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we can probably still get the two-bedroom place, but on a fixed-rate deal we can pay from her wage alone. She'd laugh at me for doing a spreadsheet of it. I'd do the spreadsheet anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you're slow to change. What would actually make you start in 2032 and not 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing it down, honestly, and telling the union branch so they hold me to it. If I just promise myself, I'll slide. If Femi and the others are checking on me, I'll go.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to win **retraining money** and shorter weeks.
I'd post more than usual, because a decade is long enough to **change the law**.
think: I'd qualify and maybe get decent, then face AGI at **thirty-seven**.
My biggest risk is **wasting the decade** by telling myself it's far away.
do: Qualify and aim for a **manager role** by thirty.
Save towards **a year of bills** by 2030.
Start **hands-on retraining** in 2032, so I get the robot years as well.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, because time is what a slow changer needs.
S4.quote: A decade sounds like loads of time, but I know myself. I'd waste ten years telling myself the robots were far away.
fieldNote: The decade lets him picture a **real career** first, and he sounds noticeably calmer.
He knows his own **tendency to slide** and wants the union branch to hold him to a date.
He'd still plan the flat around his partner's **single wage**, which shows how sure he is the job ends.

steps.text: Save towards a full year of bills by 2030
Start retraining for hands-on hospital work in 2032
Ask the union branch to hold him to the 2032 date
Buy the two-bedroom flat only on Lena's wage alone

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Not because it's the worst end point, they all end the same, but because I'd have no time, and I need time. What would help is a proper redundancy deal for trainees and paid retraining, real money, not a website with free videos. And the union having a say before the firm signs anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be bad at something right when it's being automated. Everyone talks about experts losing jobs. Nobody asks about the people still learning accounting, who'll never get to be good at it.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks about the people still learning accounting, who'll never get to be good at it.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old junior** preparing accounts and tax returns for sole traders and small landlords.
He failed a **tax exam** last spring and refuses the firm's bank-feed tool, so he feels slowest on the floor.
He blames **firm partners** for cuts and turns to the union as the change gets faster.
His nurse partner's **hands-on job** becomes the household's safety net in every AGI picture.
More time makes him calmer, but he knows he'd **wait too long** to move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time and he needs time to change.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **trainee redundancy deal** and paid retraining with real money behind it.
The **union having a say** before the firm signs any AI contract.
